rv.q: It's eye-opening, generous and brilliantly inventive.
When the acting is as good as it is here the result is a thrilling suspension of disbelief; we're aware of the artifice but also experience it as authentic.

Overall this is a terrific piece of work. It's fine-grained, deftly edited, unshowily framed by Evans and set designer Vicki Mortimer to focus on the performers and the real-life stories they are telling.

“Well I can’t roll with, like, my nails on, yeah, ’cos my nails are, like, longer than my future,” complains 16-year-old Mia (Sarita Gabony) as she tries to coax her boyfriend into rolling her a cigarette.
At three hours 40 minutes with two intervals, this is a baggy, vivacious first draft, in need of cutting.
Appealing as these kids are, Our Generation goes nowhere new thematically or dramatically.
Our Generation is an experiment that, though steered by some phenomenally assured performances, collapses under its own weight.

Still, if the running time could easily be cut by half, I haven't seen such assured displays of youthful energy since this auditorium played host to Lee Hall's magnificent teenage odyssey Our Ladies of Perpetual Succour six years ago.
But gosh it's boring. Patronising too.
Director Daniel Evans makes this mini-epic brim with the buoyancy and flair that have characterised his work over the years.
It is a remarkable piece of lively theatre packed with charismatic performances.
My main criticism preventing me from raving about Our Generation is that the play runs long. Very long. 3 hours and 40 minutes to be more precise, including two intervals.

The show could use a little more of this overt questioning of the social, political and family structures that shape their lives: it is all there but more exploration of the consequences for them and us would make Our Generation stronger.
But as a piece of theatre, it is heavy going, its sheer ambition also its greatest weakness.
